claims.text: The enhanced corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a deliberately applied surface treatment or cladding.
The applied treatment forms a thin, uniform, and chemically inert barrier.
The barrier limits ingress of corrosive species.
A chromium-based cladding or similar surface treatment can form a continuous, adherent barrier on steel.
Coating integrity, thickness, and homogeneity govern its effectiveness as a physical and chemical barrier.
The coating prevents direct contact between corrosive species and the steel substrate.
Preventing contact between corrosive media and the substrate reduces the rate of electrochemical corrosion reactions.
Coated steel samples will have lower weight loss than uncoated samples under identical corrosive conditions.
Coated steel samples will develop smaller pits than uncoated samples under identical corrosive conditions.
The proposed protective mechanism should hold for steels of standard compositions under moderate corrosive conditions typical of many chemical-processing and nuclear applications.
Under extremely aggressive chemical conditions, factors other than the coating barrier may dominate corrosion behavior.
Radiation-induced loss of coating integrity may cause factors other than the coating barrier to dominate corrosion behavior.
Threshold coating thickness and adherence quality required for protection have not been quantified.
Long-term coating durability under high-dose radiation remains uncertain.
Failure of coated samples to show a statistically significant corrosion-rate reduction relative to uncoated controls would falsify the proposed governing-cause hypothesis.
